questions.prompt: What is a credit score?
choices: A number that predicts how likely you are to repay borrowed money
The amount of money in your bank account
A tax the government charges on loans
The interest rate on your savings account
questions.explanation: A credit score is a snapshot of your borrowing trustworthiness, so lenders can guess how risky it is to lend to you.

questions.prompt: A FICO credit score ranges from a low of 300 up to a high of what number?
questions.explanation: FICO scores run from 300 to 850 — the higher you climb, the better the rates lenders offer you.

questions.prompt: Paying your bills on time is the single biggest factor in your credit score.
questions.explanation: Payment history is about 35% of a FICO score — nothing else moves the needle more than paying on time.

questions.prompt: Sort each action into whether it's a soft inquiry (no score impact) or a hard inquiry (can ding your score).
items: Applying for a new credit card
Getting a pre-approved offer in the mail
questions.explanation: Soft inquiries — like peeking at your own score — never hurt you. Hard inquiries happen when you actually apply for credit and can shave off a few points.

questions.prompt: Which habits help you build a strong credit score? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Paying every bill on time
Keeping credit card balances low
Maxing out your cards every month
Keeping older accounts open
questions.explanation: On-time payments, low balances, and a long history all help. Maxing out cards spikes your utilization and drags your score down.

questions.prompt: Match each FICO score range to its rating.
questions.explanation: Roughly: 800+ is exceptional, 670–739 is good, 580–669 is fair, and under 580 is poor. Aim to keep climbing.

questions.prompt: A single hard inquiry usually only lowers your score by a few points.
questions.explanation: One hard inquiry is a small, temporary dip. Missing payments does far more damage than a single application.

questions.prompt: What does APR stand for on a credit card?
choices: Annual Percentage Rate
Approved Payment Return
Average Purchase Reward
Automatic Payment Reminder
questions.explanation: APR is the Annual Percentage Rate — the yearly cost of carrying a balance on your card.

questions.prompt: If you pay your full statement balance by the due date, you typically pay no interest on your purchases.
questions.explanation: That interest-free window is called the grace period — pay in full and the card is basically free to use.

questions.prompt: What is the 'minimum payment trap'?
choices: Paying only the minimum keeps you in debt for years because most of it goes to interest
The bank forces you to pay extra fees each month
You can never pay more than the minimum
The minimum payment resets your credit score
questions.explanation: Paying just the minimum barely touches the balance — most goes to interest, so the debt can linger for years.

questions.prompt: Your card has a $2,000 limit and a $500 balance. What is your credit utilization, as a percent?
questions.explanation: Utilization is balance ÷ limit: $500 ÷ $2,000 = 25%.

questions.prompt: Experts suggest keeping your credit utilization below what percent to protect your score?
questions.explanation: Staying under 30% utilization tells lenders you're not leaning too hard on your available credit.

questions.prompt: Which are smart credit card habits? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Pay the statement balance in full each month
Keep your utilization low
Only ever pay the minimum
Set up autopay for at least the minimum
questions.explanation: Paying in full, keeping balances low, and automating payments keep you safe. Paying only the minimum is the trap to avoid.

questions.prompt: Match each credit card term to its meaning.
pairs: Interest-free window if you pay in full
Smallest amount due to stay current
questions.explanation: Knowing these four terms is most of what you need to use a card without getting bitten.

questions.prompt: Match each loan term to its meaning.
pairs: The extra you pay for borrowing
Yearly cost including interest and fees
How long you have to repay
questions.explanation: Principal is what you borrow, interest is the price of borrowing it, and the term is how long you take to pay it back.

questions.prompt: You borrow $1,000 at 5% simple interest for 1 year. How much interest do you owe?
questions.explanation: Simple interest is principal × rate × time: $1,000 × 5% × 1 = $50.

questions.prompt: You borrow $1,000 at 5% simple interest, but now for 2 years. How much total interest do you owe?
questions.explanation: $1,000 × 5% × 2 years = $100 — double the time means double the interest.

questions.prompt: With a fixed-rate amortizing loan, your early payments go mostly toward interest and later payments go mostly toward principal.
questions.explanation: Early on you owe interest on a big balance, so most of the payment is interest. As the balance shrinks, more of each payment chips away the principal.

questions.prompt: What is the principal of a loan?
choices: The original amount you borrowed, before interest
The interest you pay each month
The bank that gave you the loan
The penalty for paying late
questions.explanation: The principal is the starting amount you borrowed — interest is charged on top of it.

questions.prompt: Same loan amount and same interest rate — order these from LEAST total interest paid to MOST.
questions.explanation: The longer you take to repay, the more total interest you rack up — even if the monthly payment feels smaller.

questions.prompt: All else equal, which loan will cost you the most in total interest?
choices: A higher APR with a longer term
A lower APR with a shorter term
A lower APR with a longer term
A higher APR with a shorter term
questions.explanation: A higher rate and more time both pile on interest — combine them and you pay the most overall.

questions.prompt: Sort each into 'Usually good debt' or 'Usually bad debt'.
items: Credit card debt for a vacation
questions.explanation: Good debt buys things that build wealth or income at a reasonable rate. Bad debt is high-cost borrowing for things that lose value or get used up.

questions.prompt: What generally makes a debt 'good' debt?
choices: It helps you build wealth or income and usually has a lower interest rate
It always has to be paid back quickly
It comes from a friend instead of a bank
It never charges any interest
questions.explanation: Good debt is an investment in your future — like a home or education — at a manageable interest rate.

questions.prompt: Payday loans often carry extremely high APRs, sometimes around 400%.
questions.explanation: Payday loans look small but their fees translate to sky-high APRs — that's why they're classic bad debt.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to 'default' on a loan?
choices: Failing to make your payments as agreed
Paying the loan off early
Refinancing to a lower rate
Making an extra payment
questions.explanation: Defaulting means you've stopped paying as promised — a serious step that hurts your credit and can trigger collections.

questions.prompt: Which are possible consequences of defaulting on a loan? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Damage to your credit score
Your account sent to collections
Possible wage garnishment
Your credit score automatically jumps to 850
questions.explanation: Default can wreck your credit, send your debt to collectors, and even lead to garnished wages. It definitely won't boost your score.

questions.prompt: Match each debt to how it's usually classified.
questions.explanation: Low-rate borrowing that builds an asset tends to be good; high-rate borrowing for spending tends to be bad.

questions.prompt: A payday lender charges $15 in fees for every $100 borrowed. On a $200 loan, how many dollars in fees do you pay?
questions.explanation: $15 per $100 × 2 = $30 in fees for just two weeks — which works out to a shockingly high APR.

questions.prompt: In the debt 'avalanche' method, which debt do you attack first?
choices: The one with the highest interest rate
The one with the smallest balance
The newest debt you took on
The one with the friendliest lender
questions.explanation: The avalanche targets the highest interest rate first, which saves you the most money over time.

questions.prompt: In the debt 'snowball' method, which debt do you pay off first?
choices: The one with the smallest balance
The one with the highest interest rate
The largest debt you owe
Whichever is due first
questions.explanation: The snowball knocks out the smallest balance first, giving you a quick win to stay motivated.

questions.prompt: The avalanche method saves you the most money in interest over time.
questions.explanation: By killing the highest-rate debt first, the avalanche minimizes the total interest you pay.

questions.prompt: Why do some people prefer the snowball method even though it can cost a little more?
choices: Quick early wins keep them motivated to keep going
It's the only method banks allow
It always pays off debt faster than avalanche
It erases interest completely
questions.explanation: Paying off a whole debt fast feels great, and that momentum helps many people stick with the plan.

questions.prompt: You're using the avalanche method. Order these debts by which you'd pay off first (highest rate first).
questions.explanation: Avalanche always chases the highest interest rate first, then works down — that's the cheapest path out.

questions.prompt: Which are smart steps when getting out of debt? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Always pay at least the minimum on every debt
List your debts with their rates and balances
Stop making any payments until you've saved a lump sum
Put any extra money toward one target debt at a time
questions.explanation: Always cover every minimum, map out your debts, and focus extra cash on one target. Skipping payments just adds fees and damages your credit.

questions.prompt: Match each payoff idea to its defining rule.
pairs: Pay on every debt to avoid penalties
questions.explanation: Snowball chases small balances, avalanche chases high rates, and minimums keep every account in good standing while you focus your extra money.

questions.prompt: What does a higher credit score generally mean for you?
choices: Lenders see you as less risky and may offer lower interest rates
You must borrow more money each year
Your bank balance is automatically higher
You never have to pay interest again
questions.explanation: A higher score signals you repay reliably, so lenders reward you with better rates and easier approvals.

questions.prompt: A credit card has a $1,000 limit and a $200 balance. What is your credit utilization, as a percent?
questions.explanation: Utilization is balance ÷ limit: $200 ÷ $1,000 = 20%, comfortably under the 30% guideline.

questions.prompt: Paying only the minimum on a credit card can keep you in debt for years.
questions.explanation: Most of a minimum payment goes to interest, so the balance barely shrinks — that's the minimum payment trap.

questions.prompt: Sort each into 'Good debt' or 'Bad debt'.
items: Credit card debt for impulse buys
questions.explanation: Low-rate borrowing that builds an asset is good debt; high-rate borrowing for spending is bad debt.

questions.prompt: If you pay your full statement balance by the due date, what usually happens?
choices: You owe no interest on those purchases
Your interest rate doubles
Your credit limit is lowered
You're charged a late fee
questions.explanation: Paying in full within the grace period means your purchases cost you nothing extra in interest.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.explanation: These four terms cover payoff strategies plus the basics of what a loan actually costs.

questions.prompt: You borrow $500 at 6% simple interest for 1 year. How much interest do you owe?
questions.explanation: Simple interest is principal × rate × time: $500 × 6% × 1 = $30.

questions.prompt: Which of these help improve your credit score? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Making on-time payments
Keeping utilization low
Maxing out your cards
Having a long credit history
questions.explanation: On-time payments, low utilization, and a long history all lift your score. Maxing out cards does the opposite.

questions.prompt: Using the avalanche method, order these debts by which you'd pay off first (highest rate first).
questions.explanation: Avalanche attacks the highest interest rate first, then works down to save the most money.

questions.prompt: Defaulting on a loan can hurt your credit and send the debt to collections.
questions.explanation: Default is a serious step — it damages your credit score and can hand your debt over to collectors.
